1a.html:
Ore dressing (mineral processing) removes most of the gangue from the ore by mainly physical methods, giving a concentrate rich in the value mineral and tailings. It is done before extraction because:

  1. Ores are lean mixtures. The value mineral is finely intergrown with gangue, and often only about 1% of the ore is metal. Smelting or leaching the whole ore would mean heating, fluxing or dissolving mostly waste rock.
  2. Lower extraction cost and energy: the tonnage to be heated or chemically treated falls, so fuel, flux, reagent and energy fall. Upgrading 1% Cu ore to a 25% Cu concentrate cuts the feed about 25-fold.
  3. Saving in freight: the gangue is discarded at the mine, so far less tonnage is shipped to the smelter.
  4. Smaller metal losses: less gangue gives less slag, and so less metal lost in it.
  5. Purer metal: fewer impurities reach the extraction step, so the crude metal is purer and refining easier.
  6. Expansion of ore reserves: rock below 1% Cu was not processed in the last century; today 0.5% Cu rock is.
  7. Complex ores: selective beneficiation gives separate Cu, Pb and Zn concentrates, each treated by its own route.

These gains must outweigh the dressing cost and the metal lost to the tailings.
pts: States that ore dressing removes gangue by (mainly physical) methods, giving a concentrate and tailings, before extraction
Ores are lean, fine-grained mixtures, so treating the whole ore would mean heating or leaching mostly waste
Reduced tonnage lowers extraction cost (fuel, flux, reagent, energy), with a number such as about 25-fold less feed
Saving in freight because the gangue is discarded at the mine
Smaller metal losses because less slag is made
Expansion of ore reserves: 1% Cu once the limit, 0.5% Cu rock processed today
A further reason: purer crude metal, or separate concentrates from complex Cu-Pb-Zn ores, with the caveat of dressing cost and tailings losses
1a.src: Introduction (sources, recycling, overview), slides 29-30, 34; Book Ch 1 reading, pp 25-28
1a.watch:
• "Why" wants reasons, each with its mechanism (less tonnage, less slag); a list of dressing methods does not answer it.
  • Quote the slide figure: 1% to 0.5% Cu. It is the standard example of how dressing expands the reserves.
  • Hard-to-treat ores that do not respond to dressing are processed directly, for example by leaching.

1b.html:
Motion of the charge. A ball mill is a cylinder turning about a horizontal axis, charged with ore and hard steel or ceramic balls. As the shell rotates, the charge is lifted up the side of the lining and then falls back under gravity through a variety of trajectories. Most of the reduction is done by impact as balls drop from near the top of the shell; the rest is by abrasion where particles rub.

Zones where size reduction occurs

  1. Zone A, the rising charge against the lining. Most of the charge is lifted with the shell, but some particles move in the opposite direction (shearing). Particles rub and are squeezed: size reduction by abrasion and impact.
  2. Zone B, the tumbling surface. Particles move in the same direction as their neighbours but are in intimate contact and tumble over each other (cascading). This is the major grinding zone, by abrasion and impact.
  3. Zone C, the impact zone (toe). Balls and particles that have fallen freely from the opposite side strike the charge. Size reduction here is solely by impact, which breaks the coarser particles.

Zones where there is no size reduction

  1. The free-fall region. Balls thrown from the shoulder fly through the empty space of the mill. There is no significant contact between particles in flight, so no size reduction occurs until they reach the impact zone.
  2. Regions where centrifugal action neutralises weight. At the shoulder the charge rides with the lining, with little relative motion, until it leaves the shell; little grinding happens there.
  3. Impact on the liner. Balls that overshoot the toe and strike the bare liner do no useful grinding and greatly increase liner wear.

What sets the size of the zones

  • Speed: too low, the balls only roll down (cascading) and grinding is limited; at or above the critical speed, N_c = 42.3/\sqrt{D} rpm, the whole charge centrifuges and there is hardly any grinding. Mills run at 65 to 82% of N_c.
  • Charge filling: 30 to 50% of the mill volume; it fixes the share of particles in each zone.
  • Liners: profiled liners lift the charge higher at a given speed; they reduce shearing but increase the vigorous reduction in zone B.
pts: Labelled diagram: shell and rotation direction, charge with shoulder and toe, free-fall trajectories, zones A, B, C and the no-grinding region marked
Describes the motion: charge lifted up the lining and falling back under gravity; impact of falling balls does most of the reduction
Zone A: lifted with the shell, some opposite movement (shearing), reduction by abrasion and impact
Zone B: particles in intimate contact tumbling over each other; the major grinding zone
Zone C: impact zone at the toe, reduction solely by impact from particles that fell from the opposite side
No size reduction in free fall because particles in flight do not touch
No size reduction where centrifugal action neutralises weight (charge rides with the shell), or where balls hit the bare liner (wear only)
Effect of speed: cascading when too slow, centrifuging at or above N_c; operation at 65 to 82% of N_c
Effect of charge filling (30 to 50%) and liner profile on the zones
1b.sketch:
• Shell cross-section with lifters and the direction of rotation.
  • Charge carried up the rising side to the shoulder, sloping surface down to the toe.
  • Free-fall trajectories from the shoulder to the toe, labelled "no grinding".
  • Labels: A (lifted, shearing), B (major grinding zone), C (impact zone, toe), "regions where centrifugal action neutralises weight".
1b.src: Size reduction, slides 27, 29-30; Size reduction reading (book Ch 2), pp 10, 14-15
1b.watch:
• The question asks for both kinds of zone: name the no-reduction zones explicitly and give the reason (no particle contact), not only the grinding zones.
  • Keep the zone letters consistent with the sketch; the examiner will match A, B and C to the figure.
  • Same content as the "movement of charge" questions (2013-14 Q7(a), 2018-19 Q6(c)), but here the emphasis is on where breakage does and does not happen.

2a.html:
Given: coefficient of friction between rock and jaw \mu = 0.5 in one crusher and \mu = 0.2 in the other.

Find: the range of jaw angles \theta that grip and crush the particle in each case; which crusher gives the larger product, and why.

Set-up. The fixed jaw is vertical; the swing jaw makes the angle \theta with it. A lump touches both. Each jaw pushes on it with a normal force (N_1, N_2). The normal force of the inclined jaw has an upward component that tends to squeeze the lump out of the top. Friction (\mu N_1, \mu N_2) acts down along each face and resists this. The weight of the lump is neglected (it only helps).

Step 1, horizontal balance:

N_1 = N_2\cos\theta + \mu N_2\sin\theta = N_2(\cos\theta + \mu\sin\theta)

Step 2, vertical balance at the point of slipping:

\begin{aligned} N_2\sin\theta &= \mu N_2\cos\theta + \mu N_1 \\ \sin\theta &= \mu\cos\theta + \mu(\cos\theta + \mu\sin\theta) \\ \sin\theta\,(1 - \mu^2) &= 2\mu\cos\theta \end{aligned}

Step 3, limiting angle:

\tan\theta = \frac{2\mu}{1 - \mu^2} = \tan(2\arctan\mu) \quad\Rightarrow\quad \boxed{\theta \leq 2\arctan\mu, \ \text{i.e.}\ \tan\frac{\theta}{2} \leq \mu}

The same holds when both jaws lean equally (\theta/2 each).

Step 4, the two crushers:

\begin{aligned} \mu = 0.5: &\quad \theta_{max} = 2\arctan 0.5 = 2(26.57^\circ) = 53.1^\circ \\ \mu = 0.2: &\quad \theta_{max} = 2\arctan 0.2 = 2(11.31^\circ) = 22.6^\circ \end{aligned}

So the lump is gripped for 0 < \theta \leq 53.1^\circ with \mu = 0.5 and 0 < \theta \leq 22.6^\circ with \mu = 0.2. Any angle up to 22.6^\circ grips in both cases. With the usual jaw angle of 20 to 30 degrees, the \mu = 0.5 crusher can use the whole range, the \mu = 0.2 crusher only 20 to 22.6 degrees.

Which gives larger particles: the \mu = 0.2 crusher. Its jaws must be nearly parallel. For the same gape G and jaw length L, the throat opening is about G - L\tan\theta. The chamber narrows by \tan 22.6^\circ = 0.42 per unit length of jaw at most, against up to \tan 53.1^\circ = 1.33 (0.58 at a practical 30^\circ) for \mu = 0.5. So its set is wider, its reduction ratio smaller, and its product coarser. Lumps that slip upward in the low-friction crusher are also crushed less effectively.
pts: Free-body sketch of the lump with normal forces and downward friction forces at both jaws, and the jaw angle \theta
Horizontal balance: N_1 = N_2(\cos\theta + \mu\sin\theta)
Vertical balance at slipping: N_2\sin\theta = \mu N_2\cos\theta + \mu N_1
Result \tan\theta = 2\mu/(1 - \mu^2), that is \theta \leq 2\arctan\mu (or \tan(\theta/2) \leq \mu)
\mu = 0.5: gripped for \theta up to 53.1^\circ
\mu = 0.2: gripped for \theta up to 22.6^\circ
Common range: \theta \leq 22.6^\circ works for both, or relates the ranges to the practical 20 to 30 degrees
Names the \mu = 0.2 crusher as the one giving larger particles
Reason: smaller allowable angle, so less narrowing toward the throat, a wider set and a smaller reduction ratio (or slip of lumps)
2a.sketch:
• Vertical fixed jaw and inclined swing jaw at angle \theta, with a lump touching both.
  • Normal forces N_1 and N_2 into the lump; friction \mu N_1 and \mu N_2 down along the jaw faces.
2a.src: Size reduction, slides 9-10, 13; Size reduction reading (book Ch 2), pp 3-4; Standard textbook treatment
2a.watch:
• The friction limit applies to the angle between the jaws, not to each jaw separately. A student who writes \tan\theta \leq \mu for the full angle gets 26.6^\circ and 11.3^\circ, which are the half-angle values: the method earns partial credit, the numbers do not.
  • The slides give the jaw angle as 20 to 30 degrees without the friction argument, so the derivation is standard mechanics; with \mu = 0.2 even the low end of that range is close to the limit.
  • For rock on steel \mu is typically about 0.2 to 0.3, which gives limits of about 23 to 33 degrees; this is why jaw angles are kept to 20 to 30 degrees, and a wider angle lets lumps slip up and out of the chamber.

2b.html:
The harmful effects. In batch grinding a measured charge is ground for hours until all of it passes the required mesh (say 65 mesh). The mill does not confine its action to the large particles; it keeps grinding particles that are already fine enough. So:

  1. a large amount of over-ground mineral (slimes) leaves in the discharge and is difficult to treat by concentration processes;
  2. a large amount of energy is consumed in this unnecessary and harmful over-grinding.

Simply discharging the ore after a short time (continuous open-circuit grinding) avoids over-grinding but leaves considerable oversize in the product.

What can be done

  1. Closed circuit grinding (the main remedy). Run the mill continuously with a classifier or screen on its discharge. Ore passes through the mill quickly, so little is over-ground; the classifier removes the finished product and returns the oversize to the mill as the circulating load (200 to 1000% of the new feed).
  2. Stage grinding: a rod mill first, in open circuit, because the rods preferentially break the coarse particles and give a narrow product with little fine material; then a ball mill in closed circuit for the fine grinding.
  3. Grind only to the liberation size: set the classifier cut where the value mineral is liberated from the gangue.
  4. Feed control: stage crushing gives feed of the right size; a steady feed rate avoids choking while using the full capacity of the mill.
  5. Free discharge: design the mill so that particles leave as soon as they are small enough, instead of being crushed many times.
pts: States the two harmful effects: over-ground mineral (slimes) hard to concentrate, and energy wasted on over-grinding
Notes that open-circuit (short) grinding avoids over-grinding but leaves oversize in the product
Main remedy: continuous closed-circuit grinding with a classifier or screen, product removed and oversize returned to the mill
Explains why it works: rapid passage through the mill limits over-grinding while the classifier keeps oversize in the circuit (circulating load 200 to 1000%)
Stage grinding: rod mill in open circuit (breaks the coarse particles preferentially, narrow product) followed by a ball mill in closed circuit
Grind only to the liberation size (classifier cut at liberation)
Feed control: correct feed size by stage crushing and a controlled feed rate
Free discharge so particles leave as soon as they are fine enough
2b.src: Size reduction, slides 24, 26, 33, 36-40; Size reduction reading (book Ch 2), pp 10, 12, 15-17; Standard textbook treatment
2b.watch:
• Start from the harmful effects the question names; the remedies only make sense against them.
  • Closed circuit grinding carries most of the marks; a flowsheet (mill, classifier, oversize return) makes the point quickly.
  • The slides name the two harmful effects and closed circuit grinding; stage grinding and the other measures come from the book reading and standard practice.

3a.fix: • Slide 33 of the Particle selection deck (and Example 3.5 of the reading, page 20) gives the dilution as 0.428. 30/70 = 0.4286, which rounds to 0.429 (0.43); 0.428 is a truncation. Either value earns the mark.
3a.html:
Given: pulp of 30% galena, 40% quartz and 30% water by weight; specific gravity of galena 7.5, quartz 2.7, water 1.0.

Find: (i) pulp dilution, (ii) pulp density, (iii) percent solids.

Definitions. Pulp dilution is the ratio of water to solids by weight; pulp density is the weight of unit volume of pulp (\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}, numerically its specific gravity); percent solids is the weight of dry solids as a percentage of the pulp weight.

Basis: 100 g of pulp, containing 30 g galena, 40 g quartz and 30 g water.

Volumes (volume = mass / specific gravity, with water at 1\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}):

\begin{aligned} V_{\text{galena}} &= 30/7.5 = 4.00\ \mathrm{cm^3} \\ V_{\text{quartz}} &= 40/2.7 = 14.81\ \mathrm{cm^3} \\ V_{\text{water}} &= 30/1.0 = 30.00\ \mathrm{cm^3} \\ V_{\text{pulp}} &= 48.81\ \mathrm{cm^3} \end{aligned}

(i) Pulp dilution

D = \frac{\text{weight of water}}{\text{weight of solids}} = \frac{30}{30 + 40} = \frac{30}{70} = 0.429

Answer: pulp dilution = 0.43 to 1 (0.43 t of water per tonne of solids).

(ii) Pulp density

d = \frac{\text{weight of pulp}}{\text{volume of pulp}} = \frac{100\ \mathrm{g}}{48.81\ \mathrm{cm^3}} = 2.05\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}

Answer: pulp density = 2.05 (2.05\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}, 2050\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}).

(iii) Percent solids

\%\ \text{solids} = \frac{30 + 40}{100}\times 100 = 70\%

Answer: 70% solids by weight.
pts: (i) Defines pulp dilution as weight of water to weight of solids
(i) Basis of 100 g of pulp: water 30 g, solids 30 + 40 = 70 g
(i) Dilution 30/70 = 0.43 to 1 (0.428 or 0.429 equally right)
(ii) Defines pulp density as weight per unit volume of pulp
(ii) Volumes from specific gravities: galena 4.0, quartz 14.8, water 30.0, total 48.8 \mathrm{cm^3}
(ii) Pulp density 100/48.8 = 2.05\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}
(iii) Defines percent solids as weight of dry solids as a percentage of pulp weight
(iii) Uses the weight of galena plus quartz, (30 + 40)/100, not their volume
(iii) Percent solids = 70\% by weight
3a.src: Particle selection (supersedes the 72-slide version), slides 31-33; Particle selection reading 1 (book Ch 3), pp 19-21 (Example 3.5, Eq. 3.22)
3a.watch:
• Dilution uses weights, not volumes; and the density needs volumes, so divide each mass by its own specific gravity. Using one "average" specific gravity of (7.5 + 2.7)/2 is wrong.
  • Percent solids is by weight unless stated; by volume the solids are only 18.81/48.81 = 38.5\% of the pulp.
  • Cross-check with the reading's Eq. 3.22: the mixed solids have S = 70/18.81 = 3.72, and D = (S - d)/[S(d - 1)] = (3.72 - 2.05)/(3.72 \times 1.05) = 0.43, as in (i).

3b.html:
A hydrocyclone is a classifier with no moving parts that handles large volumes of slurry and splits it, by particle size and/or specific gravity, into an underflow (coarse, dense) and an overflow (fine, light, most of the water). It uses centrifugal force instead of gravity.

Construction. A conical vessel, open at its apex (underflow or spigot), is joined to a short cylindrical section with a tangential feed inlet. The top is closed by a plate through which an axial overflow pipe passes; its extension inside, the vortex finder, stops feed short-circuiting into the overflow.

Working principle.

  1. Centrifugal field. Slurry is pumped in under pressure through the tangential inlet, so it spins; the centrifugal force is about 10 to 4000 times gravity, depending on cyclone size. Settling is greatly accelerated, so fine particles can be classified at high capacity.
  2. Two opposing forces. Each particle feels an outward centrifugal force, growing with its mass, and an inward drag from the liquid flowing towards the centre to leave by the vortex finder.
  3. Outer spiral, down. Coarse and dense particles, where centrifugal force wins, are thrown to the wall and follow the downward outer spiral to the apex: underflow.
  4. Inner spiral, up. Most of the liquid leaves through the top; it drags small and light particles to the centre and up the inner spiral to the vortex finder: overflow. An air core forms along the axis.
  5. Envelope of zero vertical velocity. Between the downward outer flow and the upward inner flow lies a surface with no vertical velocity. Particles outside it go to the underflow, those inside to the overflow.
  6. Cut size d_{50}. A particle on the envelope feels equal centrifugal and drag forces and has an equal (50%) chance of reporting to either product.

Variables. The cyclone diameter mainly fixes d_{50} (smaller cyclone, finer cut). Vortex finder (about 0.35D_c) and apex (10 to 35% of D_c) diameters, cone angle (10 to 20 degrees), feed percent solids and inlet pressure also matter; throughput rises with pressure, Q = K\,V_F\,P^{0.5}\,(\mathrm{FPW})^{0.125}.

Use: closing ball-mill grinding circuits, desliming and dewatering.
pts: Defines the hydrocyclone: a classifier with no moving parts that splits a slurry by size and/or specific gravity into underflow and overflow using centrifugal force
Construction (described or sketched): cylindrical section with tangential inlet, cone with apex, top plate, overflow pipe and vortex finder (prevents short-circuiting)
Feed under pressure enters tangentially; spinning gives centrifugal forces of about 10 to 4000 g, accelerating separation
Particles feel an outward centrifugal force and an inward drag force
Coarse and dense particles go to the wall and down the outer spiral to the underflow
Most of the water leaves through the vortex finder, dragging fine and light particles up the inner spiral to the overflow; air core on the axis
Envelope of zero vertical velocity separates the two flows: outside to underflow, inside to overflow
Cut size d_{50}: particles on the envelope feel equal forces and have a 50% chance of either product
Operating and design variables: cyclone diameter (main control of d_{50}), vortex finder and apex diameters, percent solids, inlet pressure
3b.sketch:
• Cylindrical section with the tangential feed inlet; cone ending in the apex (spigot).
  • Overflow pipe and vortex finder on the axis; air core along the axis.
  • Outer spiral down (coarse, dense) to the underflow; inner spiral up (fines, water) to the overflow.
  • Dashed envelope of zero vertical velocity between them; centrifugal force outward, drag inward.
3b.src: Particle selection (supersedes the 72-slide version), slides 34, 38-44; Particle selection reading 1 (book Ch 3), pp 23-25
3b.watch:
• The drag force points inward, towards the axis, because the liquid flows inward to the vortex finder; do not draw it outward.
  • The overflow leaves at the top through the vortex finder, the underflow at the apex at the bottom; the names do not mean "liquid over a weir" as in a rake classifier.
  • Some fines always report to the underflow with the underflow water, so the real partition curve is S-shaped, not a sharp step.

4a.html:
The process is magnetic separation, which classifies minerals by their response to a magnetic field.

Classes of minerals (relative attractability, Fe = 100):

ClassExamples
Strongly magneticmagnetite 40.2, ilmenite 24.7
Weakly magneticpyrrhotite 6.7, siderite 1.8, hematite 1.3, pyrolusite 0.7
Non-magneticpyrite 0.2, sphalerite 0.2, galena 0.04, calcite 0.03

Principle. The pull on a particle of volume V and susceptibility \chi is

F = \frac{\chi V}{\mu_0}\,B\frac{dB}{dx}

so strongly magnetic particles are held by a weak field, weakly magnetic ones only by a strong, steep field, and non-magnetic ones not at all. The separator gives a magnetic path and a gravitational path, and changing the field intensity in stages splits the magnetic fraction further.

Dry belt separator worked in stages.

  1. Dry ore is fed in a uniform layer onto a conveyor belt that runs under the start of a second, upper belt carrying electromagnets above its lower run.
  2. At the pick-up end the field is strongest, so all magnetic particles are lifted onto the underside of the upper belt. Non-magnetic particles stay on the feed belt and fall off its end into the first bin.
  3. Along the upper belt the field intensity is diminished by stages. Where it drops, the weakly magnetic particles can no longer be held and fall into the second bin; the strongly magnetic particles are held to the end of the magnets and drop into the last bin.

Equivalently, the ore can be passed through separators of increasing intensity: a low-intensity drum removes magnetite first, then a high-intensity unit takes the weakly magnetic minerals, leaving non-magnetic tailings. In a cross-belt separator the feed belt carries the ore between the magnet poles, and belts running across it remove the lifted fractions to the side.

Wet or dry. Coarse lumps (120-150 mm) are treated dry; particles below 6-8 mm can be treated wet or dry, and wet works better because water stops magnetic and non-magnetic particles sticking together.

Example: an iron ore gives a magnetite concentrate, a hematite (weakly magnetic) concentrate and calcite or silica tailings.
pts: Classifies minerals as strongly, weakly and non-magnetic with examples (magnetite, hematite, galena or calcite), or the relative attractability values
States that the force depends on susceptibility and on the field and its gradient (F \propto \chi V B\,dB/dx), so weakly magnetic minerals need a strong field
Principle of two paths: magnetic particles held in the field, non-magnetic ones follow gravity
Describes the belt separator: dry feed on a belt, electromagnets over an upper belt lift the magnetic particles, non-magnetic fall off the feed belt end
Field changed by stages so weakly magnetic particles drop at the weaker stage and strongly magnetic ones at the end, giving separate fractions
Alternative sequence of increasing intensity: low-intensity removes magnetite first, high-intensity then removes weakly magnetic minerals
Mentions the cross-belt separator (feed carried between the poles, lifted fractions removed sideways)
Wet versus dry: coarse (120-150 mm) dry; below 6-8 mm wet is better because water stops particles sticking together
Gives an application with its products, for example magnetite, hematite and silica or calcite from an iron ore
4a.src: Particle selection (supersedes the 72-slide version), slides 61-67; Standard textbook treatment
4a.watch:
• "Classification" here means sorting minerals into magnetic classes, not hydraulic classification by settling velocity.
  • The slide table places ilmenite among the strongly magnetic minerals; many texts call it weakly magnetic (paramagnetic). Either is accepted if the attractability (24.7, well below magnetite) is quoted.
  • The force depends on the field gradient, not just its strength; high-gradient separators use a matrix of steel wool or balls to recover very weakly magnetic fine particles.

4b.html:
Function. A collector makes the selected mineral hydrophobic (water-repellent). Only hydrophobic particles attach to air bubbles, and most minerals are naturally hydrophilic, so the collector creates the floatability. Adsorbed on the surface, it weakens the hydrated layer between mineral and bubble, so the particle sticks to a bubble on contact.

How it works. Collectors are organic, heteropolar molecules: a polar group that reacts with the mineral surface and a non-polar hydrocarbon chain that repels water. They adsorb with the polar end on the mineral and the chain facing the solution. Once enough is adsorbed, the surface seen by the water is hydrocarbon, so a hydrophilic mineral behaves as hydrophobic. Only the surface, not the bulk, is changed.

Example. Sodium ethyl xanthate dissociates:

\mathrm{C_2H_5OCS_2Na \rightarrow C_2H_5OCS_2^- + Na^+}

The -\mathrm{S^-} of the xanthate ion bonds strongly to the cations (\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}, \mathrm{Cu^{+}}) at a sulphide surface such as galena, leaving the ethyl groups outward.

Selectivity. The collector adsorbs preferentially on the chosen mineral and so widens the difference between minerals. A higher dose raises the chance of flotation but lowers selectivity. Typical dose: 100-750 g/t, after 10-20 min conditioning.

Types.

  • Ionising, which dissociate in water: anionic (xanthates, dithiophosphates for sulphides), the most widely used, and cationic (amines).
  • Non-ionising, practically insoluble oils that coat the surface with a thin film.

pH. At each collector concentration a mineral has a critical pH above which \mathrm{OH^-} displaces the collector and the mineral will not float. With 25 mg/L sodium diethyl dithiophosphate at pH 6.5-9.5, chalcopyrite floats but galena does not.
pts: States the function: renders the selected mineral hydrophobic (water-repellent) so that it attaches to air bubbles and floats
Heteropolar structure: polar group adsorbs on the mineral and the non-polar hydrocarbon chain faces the water, so the surface behaves as hydrocarbon
Xanthate example: dissociates to \mathrm{C_2H_5OCS_2^-}, whose -\mathrm{S^-} bonds to sulphide surface cations
Selectivity: preferential adsorption on the chosen mineral; only the surface is changed; dose raises recovery
Types: ionising (anionic such as xanthates, cationic such as amines) and non-ionising oils
Critical pH: above it the mineral does not float, with the dithiophosphate chalcopyrite-galena example or another
Typical dose (100-750 g/t) or the conditioning period before flotation
4b.src: Particle selection (supersedes the 72-slide version), slides 74-80, 85, 88; Particle selection reading 4 (end-of-chapter questions), pp 3-5
4b.watch:
• Do not describe the frother: the collector acts at the mineral-water surface, the frother at the air-water surface.
  • Slide 79 prints the xanthate as \mathrm{C_2H_5OS_2Na}; the correct formula is \mathrm{C_2H_5OCS_2Na}.
  • Excess collector also floats middlings and gangue and wastes reagent; the course book uses the minimum collector dose in the rougher stage and adds more only in the scavenger.

5.fix: Slide 37 of the roasting-yield example converts 18.52 kg of Fe to "35.61 kg" of \mathrm{Fe_3O_4}. The factor is 231.5/167.6 = 1.382, so the magnetite is 25.6 kg, the yield totals about 75.4 kg instead of 85.39 kg, and the percentages on slide 38 must be recalculated from these masses.
5.html:
Given: roaster gas (vol %) \mathrm{CO_2} 1.8, \mathrm{SO_2} 7.2, \mathrm{H_2O} 0.6, \mathrm{N_2} 80.1, \mathrm{O_2} 10.3; ore 10% Cu, 34% Fe, 14% \mathrm{SiO_2}, 42% S; 4/5 of the S removed; 50 t of ore per day; coal with 76% C; ore and fuel separate, gases mixed.

Find: (a) roasted ore per day; (b) fuel as % of ore; (c) % excess air; (d) theoretical air for roasting : for fuel.

Assumptions: 1 t = 1000 kg; Cu all as \mathrm{Cu_2S}, the rest of the S as FeS, the rest of the Fe as \mathrm{Fe_2O_3}; all \mathrm{CO_2} from the coal carbon; all \mathrm{N_2} from air (21% \mathrm{O_2}, 79% \mathrm{N_2}); the \mathrm{H_2O} is moisture; 22.4 m3 per kmol at STP. Cu 63.55, Fe 55.85, S 32.06, O 16.00, C 12.01.

Per day: Cu 5000 kg, Fe 17 000 kg, \mathrm{SiO_2} 7000 kg, S 21 000 kg.

(a) Roasted ore

\begin{aligned} \text{S left} &= 0.2 \times 21\,000 = 4200\ \mathrm{kg} \\ \mathrm{Cu_2S} &= 5000 \times \tfrac{159.16}{127.10} = 6261\ \mathrm{kg}\quad (\text{S } 1261\ \mathrm{kg}) \\ \mathrm{FeS} &= (4200 - 1261) \times \tfrac{87.91}{32.06} = 2939 \times 2.742 = 8058\ \mathrm{kg}\quad (\text{Fe } 5120\ \mathrm{kg}) \\ \mathrm{Fe_2O_3} &= (17\,000 - 5120) \times \tfrac{159.70}{111.70} = 11\,880 \times 1.430 = 16\,986\ \mathrm{kg} \\ \text{roasted ore} &= 6261 + 8058 + 16\,986 + 7000 = 38\,305\ \mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}

(a) Roasted ore = 38.3 t per day (76.6% of the ore charged).

(b) Fuel

The S removed, 0.8 \times 21\,000 = 16\,800 kg, leaves as \mathrm{SO_2} (1 kmol per kmol S). \mathrm{CO_2} and \mathrm{SO_2} are in the gas in the ratio 1.8 : 7.2:

\begin{aligned} n_{\mathrm{SO_2}} &= 16\,800 / 32.06 = 524.0\ \mathrm{kmol} \\ n_{\mathrm{CO_2}} &= 524.0 \times 1.8 / 7.2 = 131.0\ \mathrm{kmol\ C} = 131.0 \times 12.01 = 1573\ \mathrm{kg\ C} \\ \text{coal} &= 1573 / 0.76 = 2070\ \mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}

(b) Coal = 2.07 t per day = 4.14% of the ore.

(c) Excess air

\begin{aligned} \text{gas} &= 524.0 / 0.072 = 7278\ \mathrm{kmol}, \qquad \mathrm{N_2} = 0.801 \times 7278 = 5830\ \mathrm{kmol} \\ \text{air} &= 5830 / 0.79 = 7379\ \mathrm{kmol}\ (= 165\,300\ \mathrm{m^3\ at\ STP}), \qquad \mathrm{O_2\ supplied} = 0.21 \times 7379 = 1549.7\ \mathrm{kmol} \end{aligned}

Oxygen is consumed only by the products that contain oxygen; \mathrm{Cu_2S} and FeS need none.

\begin{aligned} \text{roasting: } \mathrm{S} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{SO_2} &: 524.0\ \mathrm{kmol} \\ 4\,\mathrm{Fe} + 3\,\mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\,\mathrm{Fe_2O_3} &: 0.75 \times 11\,880/55.85 = 0.75 \times 212.7 = 159.5\ \mathrm{kmol} \\ \text{roasting total} &= 683.6\ \mathrm{kmol\ O_2} \\ \text{fuel: } \mathrm{C} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_2} &: 131.0\ \mathrm{kmol\ O_2} \\ \text{theoretical} &= 683.6 + 131.0 = 814.6\ \mathrm{kmol\ O_2} \\ \text{excess} &= \frac{1549.7 - 814.6}{814.6} \times 100 = 90.2\% \end{aligned}

(c) Excess air = about 90% (90.2%) over the theoretical for roasting and combustion.

(d) Ratio of theoretical air

Both demands are met by the same air, so the air ratio equals the oxygen ratio:

\frac{683.6}{131.0} = 5.22

(d) Theoretical air for roasting : for the fuel = 5.22 : 1.

6a.html:
The leaching reagent R reacts at the mineral surface to give a soluble metal species M and other products P. Two situations can arise (see the sketches).

(a) The mineral dissolves completely. All the products are soluble, so the surface simply recedes and no solid layer forms, for example \mathrm{ZnO + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow ZnSO_4 + H_2O}. Across the liquid boundary film the reagent falls from [R]_B in the bulk to [R]_S at the surface, while M and P are highest at the surface and fall to [M]_B and [P]_B. Kinetic steps:

  1. diffusion of R from the bulk of the solution to the mineral-solution interface;
  2. reaction of R with the mineral surface to form the soluble metal species;
  3. diffusion of M (and P) away from the interface into the bulk.

(b) The mineral decomposes and dissolves in parts. An insoluble product, or the undissolved part of the ore, stays behind as a porous residue around the unreacted mineral; leaching goes on only if this layer is porous. Example: \mathrm{CaWO_4(s) + CO_3^{2-} \rightarrow CaCO_3(s) + WO_4^{2-}}. I is the mineral-residue interface and II the residue-solution interface. Kinetic steps:

  1. diffusion of R from the bulk to the residue-solution interface II;
  2. diffusion of R through the porous residue to I;
  3. reaction of R with the mineral at I to form soluble M;
  4. outward diffusion of M and P through the porous layer;
  5. diffusion of M and P from II into the bulk.

Case (a) lacks steps 2 and 4. The slowest step, or a combination, controls the rate.

Accelerating the leaching. Find the rate-controlling step first, then:

  • Film diffusion (steps 1 or 5): stir the solution. The boundary layer thins and the gradients steepen, so the rate rises with stirring speed until it levels off.
  • Chemical reaction (step 3): agitation has no effect. Raise the temperature (activation energy about 10 to 25 kcal/mol, so the rate is very sensitive to it), the reagent concentration (by the reaction order) or the oxidant supply, for example oxygen pressure.
  • Pore diffusion (steps 2 and 4): grind finer, which shortens the path and raises the surface area (10 mm to 0.1 mm gives 100 times the area per unit mass), or roast first to make the solid porous.
  • A higher temperature speeds up all the steps, diffusion only weakly (5 kcal/mol or less).
pts: Sketch (a): mineral, solution and boundary film, with [R] rising from [R]_S to [R]_B and [M], [P] falling from the surface to the bulk
Sketch (b): mineral, porous residue with interfaces I and II, and the [R], [M], [P] profiles across residue and film
Explains situation (a): complete dissolution with soluble products and no solid layer, with an example
Explains situation (b): partial decomposition leaving a porous residue (leaching goes on only if it is porous), with an example
Three steps for (a): diffusion of R in, surface reaction, diffusion of M and P out
Five steps for (b): film diffusion of R, pore diffusion of R, reaction at I, pore diffusion of M and P, film diffusion of M and P
Stirring speeds up leaching when film diffusion (step 1 or 5) controls, but has no effect when the chemical reaction (step 3) controls
Raising the temperature speeds up all steps, the chemical reaction most (activation energy about 10 to 25 kcal/mol against 5 kcal/mol or less for diffusion)
A further method tied to its step: finer grinding (surface area, shorter pore path), higher reagent or oxidant concentration, or roasting to make the solid porous

• (a): hatched mineral, solution, liquid boundary film; [R] rising from [R]_S at the surface to [R]_B; [M] and [P] falling from [M]_S, [P]_S to the bulk.
  • (b): mineral, porous residue between interfaces I and II, solution; [R] rising from [R]_I through [R]_{II} to the bulk; [M] and [P] falling from I to II to the bulk.

6a.watch:
• The slides number the steps of case (b) 1 to 5 and say "step 1 or step 5" for film diffusion and "step 3" for the reaction; in case (a) these are its steps 1, 3 and 2. Keep your numbering consistent with your sketch.
  • Even when more stirring stops helping, diffusion across the limiting film may still control; the activation energy (diffusion 5 kcal/mol or less, reaction 10 to 25 kcal/mol, that is 21 and 42 to 105 kJ/mol) tells which.
  • Extra depth: for a shrinking particle of radius R_0, the time for complete leaching grows as R_0 under reaction control and as R_0^2 under diffusion through a residue layer, so grinding helps most when pore diffusion controls.

6b.html:
Zone refining purifies a metal that is already fairly pure. A narrow molten zone is moved slowly along a solid bar; impurities that lower the melting point collect in the liquid, travel with the zone to the far end, and that end is cut off. It gives ultra-pure Si, Ge, Ga and Al.

Technique. The partly purified bar or rod is held horizontally or vertically in an inert container under inert gas or vacuum. A ring heater melts a short zone at one end and moves slowly along the bar: the zone melts impure charge at its front, and crystallised solid freezes at its back.

Principle from the phase diagram. When the impurity lowers the melting point, the liquidus and the solidus both fall from T_m of the pure metal, the solidus more steeply. At every temperature the solid holds less impurity than the liquid in equilibrium with it:

k = \frac{C_S}{C_L} < 1

A melt of composition X (C_0) starts to freeze at L_1 and deposits solid S_1 with only kC_0; the rejected impurity enriches the liquid towards L_2.

Effect of the moving zone. The solid freezing at the back of the zone is purer than the zone liquid, so the rejected impurity stays in the zone and is carried forward. After one pass (Pfann):

\frac{C_S}{C_0} = 1 - (1 - k)\,e^{-kx/l}

where l is the zone length: the first solid holds kC_0, and the last zone length freezes impure and is cropped.

Multiple passes. Passes are repeated in the same direction; the more passes, the purer the starting end. For k = 0.3 the start holds 0.3C_0 after one pass and about 0.01C_0 after five. Several heaters along the bar give several passes at once.

Conditions. The separation is good when k is far from 1, and the zone must move slowly so that freezing stays near equilibrium. Impurities with k > 1 (they raise the melting point) move the other way, to the starting end.
pts: Defines zone refining: a narrow molten zone moved along a solid bar sweeps the impurities into the liquid and to one end, which is cut off
Technique: partly purified bar or rod in an inert container or atmosphere; a heater melts a zone at one end and moves it slowly along the length
Phase diagram: temperature against impurity concentration, liquidus and solidus falling from T_m of the pure metal, three fields labelled, tie lines S_1L_1 and S_2L_2
States from the diagram that the solid holds less impurity than the liquid in equilibrium, k = C_S/C_L < 1 (S_1 purer than L_1)
The purer solid freezes at the back of the zone, the rejected impurity stays in the zone and is carried forward; the last part is impure and cropped
Multiple passes in the same direction raise the purity at the starting end
First solid holds kC_0, or quotes the Pfann single-pass equation
A condition or use: k far from 1, slow zone travel, impurities with k > 1 move to the starting end, or products such as Si, Ge, Ga

• Axes: temperature (vertical) against impurity (solute) concentration (horizontal).
  • Liquidus and solidus both falling from T_m of the pure metal, the solidus below and steeper.
  • Fields labelled Liquid, Solid + Liquid, Solid.
  • Vertical line X for the melt C_0; tie line S_1 L_1 where freezing starts and S_2 L_2 where it ends.

6b.watch:
• The phase diagram carries the marks for "principles": label the axes, both lines and the tie line, and say which composition is the solid.
  • Do not say the impurity "evaporates" or is "removed" in the zone: it is only redistributed along the bar, and the impure end must be cut off.
  • Fast zone travel lets the rejected impurity build up ahead of the freezing front, so the effective k moves towards 1 and each pass removes much less impurity.
  • Extra depth: silicon is refined by the floating-zone method (no container) because molten Si reacts with crucible materials and picks up oxygen and other contamination; after many passes the profile reaches a limiting (ultimate) distribution, set by k and the zone length.

7a.fix: • Slide 65 (and the course book p 28) writes the elution step as \mathrm{R_4UO_2(SO_4)_3 + 4Cl \rightarrow 4RCl + UO_2(SO_4)}. Sulphur (3 against 1) and charge do not balance, and chloride must be \mathrm{Cl^-}. The uranium returns to solution as \mathrm{[UO_2(SO_4)_3]^{4-}}, or equivalently \mathrm{UO_2SO_4 + 2SO_4^{2-}}, as written in the Answer. The book's loading equation also prints \mathrm{2SO_3^{-4}} for \mathrm{2SO_4^{2-}}.
7a.html:
Why the leach liquor is purified

Leaching is rarely completely selective, so the pregnant liquor also carries ions that interfere with later steps or would leave unacceptable impurity levels in the product. Purification lowers their concentration, or removes the desired metal selectively and leaves the impurities behind. The common methods are selective precipitation, ion exchange and solvent extraction.

Principle

Metal ions in solution exchange with specific ions held by a solid (a resin) or by a second liquid phase. The exchange is reversible and stoichiometric, so it can (i) remove unwanted ions from the solution and (ii) concentrate a selected metal ion.

The resin is an insoluble, chemically stable, rigid 3-D polymer framework, made as small hard porous beads (0.5-1 mm) of high surface area. Functional groups bonded to the framework supply the exchangeable ions: the framework fixes the physical properties, the functional groups control the selectivity.

\begin{aligned} \text{cation exchanger:}&\quad \mathrm{2\,R{-}SO_3H + Cu^{2+} \rightleftharpoons (R{-}SO_3)_2Cu + 2H^+}\\ \text{anion exchanger:}&\quad \mathrm{R^+Cl^- + A^- \rightleftharpoons R^+A^- + Cl^-} \end{aligned}

The cycle

  1. Loading (sorption): clear pregnant liquor flows through columns of resin; the resin takes up the metal ion and releases its own ion. The barren solution is dumped.
  2. Elution (stripping): a relatively small volume of strong solution reverses the reaction, giving a concentrated, pure eluate.
  3. Regeneration: the resin is returned to its original form, ready for sorption again.

Example: uranium from sulphuric acid leach liquor

Uranium forms the complex anion \mathrm{[UO_2(SO_4)_3]^{4-}}, while the impurity metals are mostly cations, so an anion-exchange resin takes up the uranium and leaves the impurities in solution. Low-grade ores (about 0.2 % \mathrm{U_3O_8}) are treated this way.

\begin{aligned} \text{loading:}&\quad \mathrm{[UO_2(SO_4)_3]^{4-} + 2R_2SO_4 \rightarrow R_4UO_2(SO_4)_3 + 2SO_4^{2-}}\\ \text{elution (acidified chloride):}&\quad \mathrm{R_4UO_2(SO_4)_3 + 4Cl^- \rightarrow 4RCl + [UO_2(SO_4)_3]^{4-}}\\ \text{regeneration:}&\quad \mathrm{4RCl + 2H_2SO_4 \rightarrow 2R_2SO_4 + 4HCl} \end{aligned}

Plant practice (resin-in-column)

Columns A and B load in series while C is eluted. When A is saturated it goes to elution, B leads and the freshly eluted C becomes the tail; the change-overs repeat endlessly. The flow is counter-current: fresh liquor meets nearly loaded resin, and fresh resin meets nearly exhausted liquor.

Why it purifies and concentrates

Ions the resin does not take stay in the barren solution (purification). Loading and elution are almost 100 % efficient, so the concentration factor is about V_{\text{liquor}}/V_{\text{eluate}} (concentration). The exchange depends on the size and valence of the ions, their concentration, the nature of the resin and the temperature.
pts: Need for purification: leaching is not selective, impurities interfere or contaminate the product; ion exchange is one of the methods (with selective precipitation and solvent extraction)
Principle: ions in solution exchange with ions held on a solid resin (or a second liquid); reversible and stoichiometric; removes unwanted ions or concentrates a selected one
Resin: insoluble, chemically stable 3-D polymer framework as porous beads (about 0.5-1 mm); bonded functional groups supply the exchangeable ions and control selectivity
A general exchange reaction for a cation or an anion exchanger, for example \mathrm{2R{-}SO_3H + Cu^{2+} \rightleftharpoons (R{-}SO_3)_2Cu + 2H^+}
The cycle: loading in columns, elution with a small volume of strong solution to give a concentrated eluate, regeneration of the resin
Uranium is the complex anion \mathrm{[UO_2(SO_4)_3]^{4-}} while impurities are cations, so an anion resin is selective
Uranium reactions for loading, elution with chloride and regeneration (1 each; elution balanced with the uranyl sulphate complex, or \mathrm{UO_2SO_4 + 2SO_4^{2-}})
Plant: resin in tall columns, A and B loading in series while C is eluted, then change-over; counter-current contact
Purification (impurity ions stay in the barren solution) and concentration (eluate volume much smaller, nearly 100 % efficient steps)
Factors: ion size and valence, concentration, nature of the resin, temperature

• The same question was set in 2014-15 (3b) and 2016-17 (2b). "Methods" in the plural is covered by the resin (liquid-solid) method and, briefly, exchange with a second liquid phase (amine extractants, see solvent extraction).
  • No sketch is asked, so none is credited; the column figure only shows the change-over.
  • In the uranium equations \mathrm{R^+} is the fixed quaternary ammonium group of the anion resin, so \mathrm{R_2SO_4} is the resin in its sulphate form and RCl in its chloride form.

7b.html:
Separating the pregnant solution

Leaching gives a pregnant leach liquor and a solid residue of gangue. Fine particles stay in suspension, and later steps need a clear liquor.

  1. Coarse ore (heap, dump, percolation or vat leaching): the solution drains through the bed and is drawn off below it or collected in a pond; the bed is then washed with water.
  2. Fine ore (agitation leaching): the slurry needs solid-liquid separation:
    • Thickening (decantation): slurry enters through a central feed well; solids settle, and the clear overflow (pregnant solution) runs into a launder. Slow rakes move the underflow to a central discharge; flocculants (lime, glue) speed settling.
    • Filtration of the underflow on a rotary vacuum drum filter or a filter press.
    • A final clarifying filtration removes the remaining suspended solids.

Minimising the losses

Tailing losses are (i) chemical, metal left undissolved, and (ii) mechanical, pregnant solution entrained in the residue (thickener underflow still holds 40-50 % liquid). In the course leaching example, 78 % of the 12.7 t of copper lost was dissolved copper in solution discarded with the wet tailings.

  • Counter-current decantation (CCD): underflow moves forward through a train of thickeners, wash water enters the last and overflow moves backward; the strongest liquor leaves the first thickener, recovering most metal with least water.
  • Wash on the filter with sprays, and dewater the residue as far as possible before discarding it.
  • Recycle weak washings to the leach, or recover their metal (for example cementation of the last wash on scrap iron).
  • Economic limit: wash until the metal left is worth less than the cost of removing it; excess water dilutes the liquor.
  • Chemical loss: fine enough grinding, enough reagent and time, and multi-stage counter-current leaching (strongest solution on the hardest-to-dissolve particles).
pts: Leaching gives a pregnant liquor and a solid residue; fine particles stay suspended and later steps need a clear liquor
Coarse ore (heap, vat, percolation): solution drains through the bed and is collected; the bed is washed
Thickening or decantation: central feed well, solids settle, clear overflow is the pregnant solution, rakes move the underflow (flocculants help)
Filtration: rotary vacuum drum filter or filter press, or clarifying filtration of the liquor
Names the two losses: chemical (undissolved metal) and mechanical (solution entrained in the residue)
Counter-current washing: underflow forward, wash water into the last thickener, solution backward; strongest liquor leaves the first stage with least water
Washing rule: wash until the value of metal left is less than the cost of recovering it (too much water dilutes the liquor)
Wash on the filter or recycle and treat the weak washings (for example cementation of the last wash)
Cuts chemical loss: grinding, reagent, time, or multi-stage counter-current leaching

8a.html:
Relative activity. The electrochemical series ranks metals by their standard reduction potential against the hydrogen electrode (0 V). The more negative E^\circ, the more reactive the metal and the harder its ion is to reduce: Au +1.50, Ag +0.80, Cu +0.34, H 0.00, Ni -0.25, Fe -0.44, Zn -0.76, Mn -1.18, Al -1.66, Mg -2.37, Na -2.71 V.

Cathode competition. In water the metal ion competes with hydrogen, and the reaction with the more positive deposition potential wins:

E_{\mathrm{M}} = E^\circ_{\mathrm{M}} + \frac{0.0592}{z}\log a_{\mathrm{M^{z+}}} - \eta_{\mathrm{M}}, \qquad E_{\mathrm{H}} = -0.0592\,\mathrm{pH} - \eta_{\mathrm{H}}

The metal deposits when E_{\mathrm{M}} > E_{\mathrm{H}}; \eta_{\mathrm{H}} is the hydrogen overvoltage on the cathode surface.

1. Metals nobler than hydrogen (Cu, Ag, Au). E_{\mathrm{M}} > E_{\mathrm{H}} even in strong acid and at low metal activity, so they deposit readily. Hydrogen appears mainly when the current density approaches the limiting current. Copper is won from about 150-180 g/L \mathrm{H_2SO_4} at 85-95 % current efficiency.

2. Less noble metals with a high hydrogen overvoltage (Zn, Cd, Pb, Sn, Mn). By equilibrium hydrogen should evolve first, but on these metals \eta_{\mathrm{H}} is about 0.7-1 V (against below 0.1 V on Pt), which pushes E_{\mathrm{H}} below E_{\mathrm{M}}. Zinc is won at 400-600 A/m^2, 35-40 ^\circC, on Al cathodes, at about 90 % efficiency, but only from a deeply purified electrolyte: Co, Ni, Sb, Ge lower \eta_{\mathrm{H}} and re-dissolve the zinc. Mn (-1.18 V) needs a near-neutral ammonium sulphate electrolyte and gives only about 60-70 %.

3. Less noble metals with a low hydrogen overvoltage (Fe, Ni, Co). They need a weakly acid (pH about 2-4), warm electrolyte, often with diaphragms, and give lower efficiency.

4. Very reactive metals (Al, Mg, Na, Ca, Li, Ti). E^\circ lies below about -1.6 V: no attainable overvoltage stops hydrogen evolution, the current goes to \mathrm{H_2}, and any metal formed reacts with water:

\mathrm{2Al + 6H_2O \rightarrow 2Al(OH)_3 + 3H_2}

Raising the pH does not help, because the hydroxide precipitates first.

Conclusion. Whether a metal can be electrowon from water is set by its potential relative to hydrogen, corrected for overvoltage, pH and concentration. The most reactive metals are won by fused-salt electrolysis: Al from cryolite-alumina, Mg from \mathrm{MgCl_2}, Na from NaCl.
pts: Explains the electrochemical series: metals ranked by E^\circ against hydrogen (0 V), more negative means more reactive, with values
At the cathode the reaction with the more positive deposition potential occurs first; metal ion and \mathrm{H^+} compete (Nernst forms for both)
Nobler metals (Cu, Ag, Au) deposit readily even from strong acid; hydrogen mainly near the limiting current
Less noble metals: thermodynamically hydrogen should be discharged first
Hydrogen overvoltage (high on Zn, Pb, Hg; low on Pt) moves the hydrogen potential below that of the metal, so Zn, Cd, Pb, Mn can deposit
Operating conditions for zinc (high current density, low temperature, pure electrolyte free of Co, Ni, Sb, Ge) and about 90 % efficiency
Fe, Ni, Co with low overvoltage need pH control and give lower efficiency
Very reactive metals (Al, Mg, Na; E^\circ below about -1.6 V): hydrogen evolves instead and the metal would react with water (balanced equation)
Concludes that such metals are won by fused-salt electrolysis, with examples (Hall-Heroult Al, Mg from \mathrm{MgCl_2}, Na from NaCl)
States the overall criterion: potential relative to hydrogen, corrected for overvoltage, pH and concentration

• The course slides for this topic were not available; this answer follows the standard textbook treatment, so check it against the lecture notes.
  • A list of the series alone earns little; the marks are for the hydrogen competition and the overvoltage argument.
  • Overvoltage values change with current density, temperature and surface; quote them as "about" and give the trend.

8b.html:
Harmful impurities in electrical-grade copper

  1. Impurities that lower conductivity (in solid solution): P, Fe, Si, As, Sb, Ti, Co, Sn, Ni. Only 0.015-0.04 % P cuts the conductivity to about 85 % IACS, against about 101 % for electrolytic tough-pitch copper. Ag, Cd, Zn have little effect.
  2. Impurities that spoil workability and annealing: Bi and Pb (grain-boundary films, hot shortness, wire breaks) and Se, Te, S (raise the softening temperature). Bi harms at a few ppm.

Grade 1 cathode allows about 65 ppm of impurities in total.

Elimination during electrorefining

Fire-refined anodes (about 99.5 % Cu) dissolve in a \mathrm{CuSO_4}-\mathrm{H_2SO_4} electrolyte (about 45 g/L Cu, 180 g/L acid, 60-65 ^\circC, about 0.3 V) and pure copper plates on the cathode:

\mathrm{Cu \rightarrow Cu^{2+} + 2e^-} \ \text{(anode)}, \qquad \mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu} \ \text{(cathode)}

The low cell voltage separates the impurities by potential:

  1. Nobler metals (Au, Ag, Pt metals) do not dissolve and fall into the anode slime; a little chloride precipitates dissolved Ag as AgCl.
  2. Se, Te as insoluble \mathrm{Cu_2Se}, \mathrm{Cu_2Te}, \mathrm{Ag_2Se}, Pb as \mathrm{PbSO_4} and Sn as a basic salt go to the slime.
  3. Base metals (Ni, Fe, Zn, Co) dissolve and stay in the electrolyte, as their deposition potentials are far below that of Cu; a bleed stream removes them.
  4. As, Sb, Bi, close to Cu in potential, can co-deposit or form floating slime. They are held low by the bleed, liberator cells and arsenate precipitation.

Addition agents (glue, thiourea) give a dense cathode that does not trap slime; the electrolyte is filtered and the current density controlled. The cathodes reach 99.99 % Cu.
pts: Impurities that lower conductivity (P, Fe, Si, As, Sb, Sn, Ni, Co), with an example of the effect (e.g. P-deoxidised Cu about 85 % IACS)
Impurities that spoil drawability or annealing (Bi, Pb, Se, Te, S), harmful at ppm level
Refining cell and reactions: crude anode, pure cathode, \mathrm{CuSO_4}-\mathrm{H_2SO_4} electrolyte, about 0.3 V
Principle: the low cell voltage separates impurities by electrode potential
Nobler metals (Au, Ag, Pt) report to the anode slime (Ag fixed by chloride)
